title: Vector Algebra in Mechanics
short_intro: Vector algebra provides the mathematical framework for describing physical quantities possessing both magnitude and direction in classical mechanics. It governs the composition and resolution of forces, velocities, accelerations, and angular quantities across inertial and non-inertial reference frames.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Addition and subtraction of vectors, resolution of vectors in Cartesian coordinates, scalar (dot) product, vector (cross) product, and condition for orthogonality or collinearity.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Triple products (scalar triple product and vector triple product), differentiation and integration of vectors with respect to time, gradient, divergence, curl, and application to central forces and Coriolis acceleration.

prerequisites: Concept of scalar and vector physical quantities

concept_notes.heading: Geometrical and Analytical Representation of Vectors
bullets: A vector is represented geometrically by a directed line segment whose length is proportional to its magnitude and direction points along the line of action.
In a three-dimensional Cartesian coordinate system, a vector A is expressed as A = A<sub>x</sub> i^ + A<sub>y</sub> j^ + A<sub>z</sub> k^, where i^, j^, and k^ are mutually orthogonal unit vectors.

The magnitude of vector A is given by |A| = sqrt(A<sub>x</sub><sup>2</sup> + A<sub>y</sub><sup>2</sup> + A<sub>z</sub><sup>2</sup>) with SI units dependent on the physical quantity represented (e.g., m s<sup>-1</sup> for velocity).

concept_notes.heading: Scalar (Dot) Product and Physical Applications
bullets: The scalar product of two vectors A and B is defined as A · B = |A| |B| cos(θ), where θ is the angle between their tails.
It yields a scalar quantity and is commutative (A · B = B · A) and distributive over vector addition.
In mechanics, the work done W by a constant force F acting through a displacement s is expressed as the scalar product: W = F · s.

concept_notes.heading: Vector (Cross) Product and Rotational Mechanics
bullets: The vector product of two vectors A and B is defined as A × B = |A| |B| sin(θ) n^, where n^ is a unit vector perpendicular to both A and B determined by the right-hand rule.
It is anti-commutative (A × B = - B × A) and non-associative.
In rotational mechanics, torque (τ), angular momentum (L), and linear velocity (v = ω × r) are formulated using the vector cross product.

concept_notes.heading: Triple Products and Differential Vector Operators
bullets: The scalar triple product A · (B × C) represents the geometric volume of the parallelepiped formed by vectors A, B, and C.
The vector triple product expands as A × (B × C) = B(A · C) - C(A · B), crucial for analyzing central forces and particle dynamics in rotating frames.
Vector differentiation with respect to a scalar parameter t yields velocity (dr/dt) and acceleration (dv/dt), while spatial derivatives involve the del operator (∇).

derivations.title: Law of Cosines and Law of Sines via Vector Addition
derivations.conditions: Triangle formed by three vectors A, B, and C such that A + B = C.
steps: Consider the vector equation C = A + B.
Take the dot product of C with itself: C · C = (A + B) · (A + B).
Expand the product: C<sup>2</sup> = A<sup>2</sup> + B<sup>2</sup> + 2A · B.
Substitute A · B = |A| |B| cos(180° - θ) = -|A||B|cos(θ) for interior angle θ, yielding the Law of Cosines: C<sup>2</sup> = A<sup>2</sup> + B<sup>2</sup> - 2AB cos(θ).

derivations.title: Expansion of Vector Triple Product
derivations.conditions: Three arbitrary vectors A, B, and C in three-dimensional space.
steps: Choose a Cartesian coordinate system such that vector B lies along the x-axis, so B = B<sub>x</sub> i^.
Let C = C<sub>x</sub> i^ + C<sub>y</sub> j^ and A = A<sub>x</sub> i^ + A<sub>y</sub> j^ + A<sub>z</sub> k^.
Compute the inner cross product B × C = (B<sub>x</sub> i^) × (C<sub>x</sub> i^ + C<sub>y</sub> j^) = B<sub>x</sub> C<sub>y</sub> k^.

Compute the outer cross product A × (B × C) = (A<sub>x</sub> i^ + A<sub>y</sub> j^ + A<sub>z</sub> k^) × (B<sub>x</sub> C<sub>y</sub> k^) = A<sub>x</sub> B<sub>x</sub> C<sub>y</sub> (-j^) + A<sub>y</sub> B<sub>x</sub> C<sub>y</sub> i^.
Rearrange and add/subtract terms involving B(A · C) - C(A · B) to obtain the invariant coordinate-free identity.
derivations.result: A × (B × C) = B(A · C) - C(A · B)

formula_sheet.name: Scalar (Dot) Product
formula_sheet.equation_html: A \cdot B = A_x B_x + A_y B_y + A_z B_z = AB \cos(\theta)
formula_sheet.variables: A, B = vectors; θ = angle between vectors
formula_sheet.conditions: Valid for any two vectors in Euclidean space

formula_sheet.name: Vector (Cross) Product
formula_sheet.equation_html: A \times B = \begin{vmatrix} i^ & j^ & k^ \\ A_x & A_y & A_z \\ B_x & B_y & B_z \end{vmatrix}
formula_sheet.variables: A<sub>x</sub>, A<sub>y</sub>, A<sub>z</sub> and B<sub>x</sub>, B<sub>y</sub>, B<sub>z</sub> = Cartesian components

formula_sheet.name: Scalar Triple Product
formula_sheet.equation_html: A \cdot (B \times C) = \begin{vmatrix} A_x & A_y & A_z \\ B_x & B_y & B_z \\ C_x & C_y & C_z \end{vmatrix}

formula_sheet.name: Vector Triple Product
formula_sheet.equation_html: A \times (B \times C) = B(A \cdot C) - C(A \cdot B)

formula_sheet.name: Time Derivative of a Vector
formula_sheet.units: Units of vector divided by seconds ([A] s<sup>-1</sup>)

formula_sheet.name: Derivative of Vector Product
formula_sheet.conditions: Differentiable vectors; order of cross product must be preserved

formula_sheet.name: Velocity via Angular Velocity
formula_sheet.variables: v = linear velocity, ω = angular velocity vector, r = position vector
formula_sheet.conditions: Rigid body rotation about a fixed point

graphs_and_experiments.title: Parallelogram Law of Vector Addition
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Two adjacent vectors P and Q originating from a common point, completed into a parallelogram with the diagonal representing the resultant R = P + Q.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Visualizes the superposition principle of concurrent forces in statics and mechanics.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in conceptual questions regarding equilibrium of concurrent forces and resultant magnitude variations.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Right-Hand Rule for Cross Product
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Right hand with fingers pointing along vector A and curling towards vector B; extended thumb pointing along the direction of A × B.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Establishes the directional orientation of axial vectors like torque and angular momentum.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Directly tested in multiple-choice questions to determine the direction of magnetic force, torque, or angular momentum.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Resolution of Vector into Orthogonal Components
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A vector A in the xy-plane making an angle θ with the x-axis, showing projections A<sub>x</sub> = A cos(θ) and A<sub>y</sub> = A sin(θ).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the independence of orthogonal spatial directions in mechanical decomposition of motion (e.g., projectile motion).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Foundation for resolving inclined plane forces and projectile kinematics.

solved_numericals.question: Find the angle between the two vectors A = 3i^ + 4j^ + 5k^ and B = 3i^ + 4j^ - 5k^.
solution_steps: Calculate the dot product: A · B = (3)(3) + (4)(4) + (5)(-5) = 9 + 16 - 25 = 0.
Apply the dot product formula: A · B = |A| |B| cos(θ).
Since A · B = 0 and magnitudes |A| and |B| are non-zero (sqrt(50) each), cos(θ) = 0.

solved_numericals.question: Determine the value of constant 'a' for which the vectors A = i^ + a j^ + 2k^, B = 2i^ - j^ + k^, and C = i^ + 2j^ - k^ are coplanar.
solution_steps: Three vectors are coplanar if their scalar triple product is zero: A · (B × C) = 0.
Set up the determinant with the components of A, B, and C: | [1, a, 2], [2, -1, 1], [1, 2, -1] | = 0.

solved_numericals.question: A particle's position vector is given by r(t) = 3cos(t) i^ + 3sin(t) j^ + 4t k^. Find the magnitude of its acceleration at any time t.
solution_steps: First differentiate the position vector r(t) with respect to time t to find velocity v(t): v(t) = dr/dt = -3sin(t) i^ + 3cos(t) j^ + 4 k^.
Differentiate velocity v(t) with respect to t to find acceleration a(t): a(t) = dv/dt = -3cos(t) i^ - 3sin(t) j^ + 0 k^.
Calculate the magnitude of acceleration: |a(t)| = sqrt((-3cos(t))<sup>2</sup> + (-3sin(t))<sup>2</sup> + 0<sup>2</sup>).
Simplify using trigonometric identity: |a(t)| = sqrt(9(cos<sup>2</sup>(t) + sin<sup>2</sup>(t))) = sqrt(9) = 3.

assumptions_and_limitations: Vector algebra assumes a flat Euclidean space (Cartesian coordinate system) unless generalized to curved Riemannian manifolds using tensor calculus.

The laws of vector addition assume that vectors obey the commutative and associative laws, which holds true for physical vectors (like forces and velocities) but fails for finite rotations of rigid bodies.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Finite rotations of a rigid body behave like vectors and obey commutative addition.
common_misconceptions.correct: Finite rotations are not vectors because they do not obey the commutative law of addition (R<sub>1</sub> + R<sub>2</sub> != R<sub>2</sub> + R<sub>1</sub>).
common_misconceptions.why: Only infinitesimal rotations act as true vectors and obey commutative vector addition.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The cross product of two vectors yields a vector whose magnitude is simply the product of their magnitudes.
common_misconceptions.correct: The magnitude of the cross product depends on the sine of the angle between them (|A × B| = AB sin(θ)).
common_misconceptions.why: The sine factor accounts for the perpendicular component, vanishing when vectors are parallel.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The scalar triple product depends on which vector is dotted and which are crossed.
common_misconceptions.correct: A · (B × C) = B · (C × A) = C · (A × B) under cyclic permutation.
common_misconceptions.why: The scalar triple product represents the signed volume of a parallelepiped, which is invariant under cyclic shifts.

quick_revision: Dot product gives scalar (AB cos(θ)); cross product gives vector (AB sin(θ) n^).
Two non-zero vectors are orthogonal if their dot product is zero, and collinear if their cross product is zero.
Scalar triple product vanishing indicates coplanarity of three vectors.
Vector triple product expansion: A × (B × C) = B(A · C) - C(A · B).
